title: Daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly aggregation
objective: Roll transactions up to a time grain (day, week, month, quarter, year) with a period key, and compute per-period counts, revenue and averages without double counting.
context: The exec dashboard has a time-series chart for every KPI: orders per month, revenue per quarter, web sessions per week. Each chart is one GROUP BY on a period key — the trick is choosing the key correctly and keeping the revenue definition consistent.

exercises.title: Orders per month
exercises.question: Ops wants a simple trend line: how many orders (of any status) were placed each month?
exercises.prompt: Return order_month (text 'YYYY-MM') and order_count (number of orders of any status) for every month that has orders, ordered by order_month ascending.
hints: The period key is strftime('%Y-%m', order_date).
GROUP BY the key, COUNT(*) the rows, ORDER BY the key.
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS order_month, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY order_month ORDER BY order_month;
exercises.why: A month key that includes the year is the backbone of every trend chart.

recall.q: Why must a month key include the year?
recall.a: Otherwise January 2024 and January 2025 collapse into one group.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT TO_CHAR(DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date), 'YYYY-MM') AS order_month, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Monthly gross revenue
exercises.question: Finance needs monthly revenue and the number of revenue-generating orders.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. Return order_month ('YYYY-MM'), valid_orders (distinct valid orders in the month) and gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals), one row per month, ordered by order_month.
hints: Join orders to order_items and filter to valid statuses before grouping.
After the join there is one row per line, so count orders with COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id).
... COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS gross_revenue ... GROUP BY order_month ORDER BY order_month
exercises.why: COUNT(*) after joining to line items counts lines, not orders — a very common inflated KPI.

recall.q: After joining orders to order_items, how do you count orders?
recall.a: COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) — COUNT(*) would count order lines.

exercises.snowflake: GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) and label with TO_CHAR(..., 'YYYY-MM').

exercises.title: Yearly revenue and average order value
exercises.question: The CFO wants a two-line summary: revenue and average order value by year.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. Return order_year (text 'YYYY'), valid_orders (distinct valid orders), gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and avg_order_value (gross revenue / valid_orders, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by order_year.
hints: Same shape as the monthly query, with strftime('%Y', ...) as the key.
AOV = total revenue / number of orders — not AVG(line revenue), which averages lines.
ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id), 2) AS avg_order_value
exercises.why: AVG(quantity*unit_price) would be average *line* value. Ratio metrics must be built from the right numerator and denominator at the right grain.

recall.q: Why is AVG(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) not the average order value?
recall.a: It averages order lines, not orders; AOV = SUM(revenue) / COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).

exercises.snowflake: YEAR(o.order_date) AS order_year (an integer) or TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'YYYY'). Division of numbers is decimal in Snowflake, so no integer-division surprise.

exercises.title: Quarterly revenue
exercises.question: The board pack reports revenue by quarter.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. Return order_quarter (text like '2025-Q1': year, '-Q', quarter number 1–4) and gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by order_quarter.
hints: Quarter number = (month + 2) / 3 with integer division.
Concatenate year, '-Q' and the quarter number with ||.
strftime('%Y', o.order_date) || '-Q' || ((CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS order_quarter
exercises.why: Custom period labels are common (fiscal quarters, half-years). Build them so they still sort chronologically as text.

recall.q: Snowflake function for the quarter number?

exercises.snowflake: SELECT YEAR(o.order_date) || '-Q' || QUARTER(o.order_date) AS order_quarter, ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; or keep DATE_TRUNC('quarter', o.order_date) as a DATE key.

exercises.title: Weekly web sessions in Q4 2025
exercises.question: Marketing wants weekly site traffic for Q4 2025.
exercises.prompt: Define the week as strftime('%Y-%W', event_time) (Monday-start weeks; '%W' week 00 holds days before the year's first Monday). For events with event_time >= '2025-10-01' and < '2026-01-01', return event_week (that 'YYYY-WW' text), sessions (distinct session_id) and events (number of event rows), ordered by event_week.
hints: event_time is a timestamp text; the half-open filter keeps all of 2025-12-31.
strftime('%Y-%W', event_time) is the week key; sessions are COUNT(DISTINCT session_id).
SELECT strftime('%Y-%W', event_time) AS event_week, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions, COUNT(*) AS events FROM web_events WHERE ... GROUP BY event_week ORDER BY event_week;
exercises.why: Weeks are the most ambiguous grain (Sunday vs Monday start, ISO weeks that straddle years). Always write the definition down next to the chart.

recall.q: Name two different 'week' definitions that give different results.
recall.a: e.g. Monday-start %W weeks vs ISO weeks (WEEKISO in Snowflake), or Sunday-start weeks; ISO week 1 can start in December.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('week', event_time) AS event_week (a DATE = Monday by default, controlled by the WEEK_START session parameter). WEEKISO(d) / YEAROFWEEKISO(d) give ISO numbering.

exercises.title: Daily site activity in December 2025
exercises.question: The web team wants a day-by-day activity table for December 2025.
exercises.prompt: For events in December 2025 (event_time >= '2025-12-01' and < '2026-01-01'), return event_date ('YYYY-MM-DD'), events (event rows), sessions (distinct session_id) and known_customers (distinct non-NULL customer_id) for each day that has events, ordered by event_date.
hints: date(event_time) truncates a timestamp to its day.
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) already ignores NULLs (anonymous visitors).
SELECT date(event_time) AS event_date, COUNT(*) AS events, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS known_customers ... GROUP BY event_date ORDER BY event_date;
exercises.why: Daily grain is where timestamps bite: grouping by the raw event_time gives one group per second. Truncate first, then group. Note days without events simply don't appear (Lesson 31 fixes gaps).

recall.q: How do you truncate a timestamp to its date in SQLite and Snowflake?
recall.a: SQLite: date(ts). Snowflake: ts::DATE or DATE_TRUNC('day', ts).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT event_time::DATE AS event_date, COUNT(*) AS events, ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

exercises.title: Monthly net revenue
exercises.question: Finance wants gross, refunds and net revenue per month, with refunds booked against the month the original order was placed.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. Refunds = SUM(returns.refund_amount) for returned lines of valid orders, assigned to the month of the original order_date. Net revenue = gross revenue − refunds (refunds = 0 when a month has none). Return order_month ('YYYY-MM'), gross_revenue, refunds and net_revenue (all rounded to 2 decimals), one row per month with valid orders, ordered by order_month.
hints: Two different grains: revenue lives on order_items, refunds on returns. Aggregate each to the month separately.
Build two CTEs keyed by order_month, then LEFT JOIN refunds onto gross (most months have no refunds).

WITH gross AS (... GROUP BY order_month), refunds AS (returns → order_items → orders ... GROUP BY order_month) SELECT g.order_month, ..., COALESCE(f.refunds, 0) ... FROM gross g LEFT JOIN refunds f ON f.order_month = g.order_month
exercises.why: Pre-aggregating each measure to the common grain before joining is THE pattern for multi-fact reporting — it avoids fan-out double counting.

recall.q: Why aggregate revenue and refunds separately before joining them?
recall.a: They live at different grains; joining raw rows first duplicates revenue or refunds (fan-out).

exercises.snowflake: Same CTE structure; key both CTEs on DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date). Snowflake's ZEROIFNULL(f.refunds) is shorthand for COALESCE(f.refunds, 0).

worked_example.question: How many orders (any status) were placed in each calendar year?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS order_year,
       COUNT(*)                     AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_year
ORDER BY order_year;
worked_example.explanation: The period key is computed per row and then used for grouping. SQLite lets you GROUP BY a SELECT alias; Snowflake does too (and also allows `GROUP BY 1`).

recipe:
**Recipe: aggregate by period in 4 moves**

1. **Build a period key** from the date: day `date(d)`, month `strftime('%Y-%m', d)`, year `strftime('%Y', d)`,
   quarter `strftime('%Y', d) || '-Q' || ((CAST(strftime('%m', d) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3)`,
   week `strftime('%Y-%W', d)` (Monday-start weeks; week `00` = days before the year's first Monday).
   Always include the **year** in the key — `'%m'` alone merges Jan 2024 with Jan 2025.
2. **Filter** to the rows that count (valid orders, a date range) in WHERE.
3. **GROUP BY the period key** and aggregate: `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)` (orders, safe after joining
   to items), `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)` (gross revenue).
4. **ORDER BY the key** — ISO-style text keys ('2025-03') sort chronologically.

```sql
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)       AS order_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)            AS valid_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS gross_revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY order_month
ORDER BY order_month;
```

**Revenue definition (course-wide):** gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over order_items of valid
orders (completed, shipped, returned). Net revenue = gross − refunds (returns.refund_amount).

**Two-measure trap:** when combining revenue (order_items grain) and refunds (returns grain), aggregate each to
the period *first*, then join the per-period results — joining raw tables first multiplies rows.
snowflake_notes:
In Snowflake the idiomatic period key is a **DATE**, not text: `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` returns
2025-03-01. Keeping it a DATE lets BI tools treat it as a time axis and lets you do DATEADD on it later.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)          AS order_month,   -- DATE 2025-03-01
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                 AS valid_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS gross_revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

| grain | SQLite key | Snowflake key |
|---|---|---|
| day | `date(d)` | `d::DATE` or `DATE_TRUNC('day', ts)` |
| week | `strftime('%Y-%W', d)` | `DATE_TRUNC('week', d)` (week start set by `WEEK_START` parameter; default Monday) |
| month | `strftime('%Y-%m', d)` | `DATE_TRUNC('month', d)`; label: `TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM')` |
| quarter | `strftime('%Y',d) \|\| '-Q' \|\| ((month+2)/3)` | `DATE_TRUNC('quarter', d)`; label `YEAR(d) \|\| '-Q' \|\| QUARTER(d)` |
| year | `strftime('%Y', d)` | `DATE_TRUNC('year', d)` or `YEAR(d)` |

Week numbering differs between systems (`%W`, ISO `WEEKISO()`, `WEEKOFYEAR()`), so always state the definition.
common_mistakes: Grouping by `strftime('%m', d)` without the year — merges the same month of different years.
COUNT(*) after joining to order_items counts lines, not orders; use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
Leaving an undefined 'week' — Sunday vs Monday start and ISO weeks give different numbers.
Grouping by a raw timestamp instead of truncating it to the day/month first.
Joining two fact tables (items and returns) before aggregating — fan-out inflates totals.
Including cancelled/pending orders in revenue — restate and apply the valid-order filter every time.
recall: Snowflake expression for a month period key that stays a DATE?
SQLite month label from a date?
What's missing from a GROUP BY month result when a month had no orders?
The month itself — it has no rows, so it doesn't appear. You need a calendar spine to show it.
